blocks.content: Picture moving into a new house and you've got two options for handling all your boxes.

Option one, you unpack every box right away. Socks go in this drawer, dishes go on that shelf, winter coats go in the hall closet, all labeled, all before you're allowed to relax. It's a lot of upfront work, but six months later you know exactly where everything is.
Option two, you just shove every box into a garage as it arrives. No sorting, no labeling. When you actually need your winter coat in December, you go dig through the garage until you find it.
A data warehouse is option one. A data lake is option two. This lesson is about the second one, when it's a smart move, and when it turns your garage into a place you're scared to open.
1. Introduction

A data lake is a large storage repository, usually built on cheap object storage, that holds data in its raw, native format. Structured rows, semi structured logs, unstructured images, all of it, side by side, with no schema forced on it upfront.

That single idea, store first, structure later, is what separates a lake from a warehouse. It sounds simple, but it changes almost everything about how teams collect, trust, and eventually use their data.

blocks.title: What you will walk away with
blocks.content: The core idea of a data lake, how schema on read differs from schema on write, why teams choose lakes anyway, the data swamp risk nobody warns you about early enough, how lakes and warehouses actually coexist in real companies, and how to reason about this tradeoff in an interview.
2. What Is a Data Lake
2.1 Raw storage, no schema upfront
A data lake stores data exactly as it arrives. No upfront modeling, no column definitions, no rejecting a record because it doesn't fit a table shape.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396321446-746236081.png
blocks.alt: Structured, semi structured, and unstructured data all landing in one data lake

blocks.content: ["Structured rows exported from an orders database, CSVs, Parquet files with a known layout","Semi structured JSON event logs, XML feeds, nested API responses","Unstructured images, video, audio, PDFs, free text support tickets"]
items: Structured rows exported from an orders database, CSVs, Parquet files with a known layout
Semi structured JSON event logs, XML feeds, nested API responses
Unstructured images, video, audio, PDFs, free text support tickets

blocks.content: All three types can sit in the same lake, in their original form, without anyone forcing them into rows and columns first.
2.2 Cheap object storage foundation

Lakes are almost always built on object storage rather than a database engine. Think Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, or Google Cloud Storage. Object storage is built for exactly this: dump in huge volumes of files cheaply, at massive scale, without worrying about schemas or indexes.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396321446-13514438.png
blocks.alt: Object storage bucket underlying a data lake, offering low cost per gigabyte and near unlimited scale

blocks.title: Why cost matters here
blocks.content: Object storage can cost a fraction of what a data warehouse charges per gigabyte. That price gap is a big part of why teams are willing to keep data around "just in case" instead of deleting it.
3. Schema on Read vs Schema on Write
blocks.text: 3. Schema on Read vs Schema on Write

blocks.content: 3.1 The warehouse way: schema on write
blocks.text: 3.1 The warehouse way: schema on write

blocks.content: A data warehouse makes you define the schema before a single row gets loaded. Column names, data types, constraints, all decided upfront. Loading data means transforming it to fit that shape first.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396321446-789840276.png
blocks.alt: Schema on write: a warehouse requires the schema to be defined before data is loaded

blocks.content: This upfront discipline is exactly why warehouse queries are fast and predictable. The structure is already there waiting for you.
3.2 The lake way: schema on read
blocks.text: 3.2 The lake way: schema on read

blocks.content: A lake flips the order. You land the raw data first, structure undefined, and only when someone actually queries it do you decide how to interpret it, using a query engine or processing job to apply structure at read time.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396321447-499283876.png
blocks.alt: Schema on read: a data lake stores data as is and applies structure only at query time

blocks.content: This means you can store data before you're sure what questions you'll ask of it later. The cost is that every reader has to figure out the structure themselves, which is slower and more error prone than a warehouse's pre baked schema.

{"headers":["Warehouse (schema on write)","Lake (schema on read)"],"rows":[["Schema defined before loading","Schema applied only when queried"],["Loading is slower, needs transformation","Loading is fast, just land the file"],["Query performance is predictable","Query performance depends on the reader"],["Rejects data that does not fit the shape","Accepts anything, in any format"]]}
4. Why Teams Want Data Lakes
4.1 Store everything cheaply, decide later

Cheap storage plus no upfront schema means you can hang on to data you're not even sure you need yet. Nobody has to make a judgment call today about whether some log field matters, because throwing it away later is easy but recreating lost history is not.
That optionality is valuable on its own. Six months from now, a product question comes up that nobody anticipated, and the raw data to answer it is already sitting there, untouched.
4.2 Use cases a rigid warehouse schema cannot support
blocks.text: 4.2 Use cases a rigid warehouse schema cannot support

blocks.content: Some workloads simply do not fit neatly into warehouse tables.

["Training a recommendation model on raw clickstream events, every field, every click, before anyone decided which columns \"mattered\"","Training an image classification model, where the data itself is a folder of images, not rows in a table","Forensic log investigation after an incident, where you need the untouched original logs, not a cleaned up summary","Experimenting with a brand new data source before committing to a fixed schema for it"]
items: Training a recommendation model on raw clickstream events, every field, every click, before anyone decided which columns "mattered"
Training an image classification model, where the data itself is a folder of images, not rows in a table
Forensic log investigation after an incident, where you need the untouched original logs, not a cleaned up summary
Experimenting with a brand new data source before committing to a fixed schema for it

blocks.content: A warehouse forces a decision about structure before you even know what you're looking for. A lake lets the data scientist or analyst make that call later, with the full raw signal still available.
5. The Real Risk: Data Swamps
5.1 How governance breaks down

Here's the catch nobody puts on the marketing slide. A data lake with no governance stops being an asset and turns into what everyone calls a data swamp: an unsearchable pile of files that nobody trusts, nobody documents, and nobody can safely use.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396322802-939280662.png
blocks.alt: A data lake without governance turning into an unsearchable data swamp

blocks.content: It happens gradually. Someone dumps a batch of files with no naming convention. Nobody records what a given folder actually contains, or who owns it, or whether it's even still accurate. A year later, three different teams have three different guesses about which dataset is the real one.

blocks.title: The gotcha
blocks.content: The absence of a schema is a feature at write time and a liability at read time. If nobody tracks what landed where, in what format, from what source, the lake becomes something people are scared to query rather than something they rely on.
5.2 Keeping a lake from becoming a swamp
blocks.text: 5.2 Keeping a lake from becoming a swamp

blocks.content: The fix isn't complicated, it just has to be deliberate.

["A data catalog that records what each dataset is, its schema (even if applied only at read time), and where it came from","Consistent naming and partitioning, for example by source and date, so files are discoverable instead of scattered","Access controls and ownership, so it's clear who is responsible for a dataset and who is allowed to read it","Lineage tracking, so you can trace a downstream table back to the raw files it was built from"]
items: A data catalog that records what each dataset is, its schema (even if applied only at read time), and where it came from
Consistent naming and partitioning, for example by source and date, so files are discoverable instead of scattered
Access controls and ownership, so it's clear who is responsible for a dataset and who is allowed to read it
Lineage tracking, so you can trace a downstream table back to the raw files it was built from

6. How Lakes and Warehouses Coexist
6.1 Raw lake in, curated warehouse out
blocks.text: 6.1 Raw lake in, curated warehouse out

blocks.content: In practice, most companies don't pick one and abandon the other. Raw data lands in the lake first. A scheduled job then cleans, filters, and aggregates a curated subset of it into a warehouse, where BI tools run fast, predictable queries for dashboards and reports.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396322804-586812150.png
blocks.alt: A curated subset of data flowing from the lake into a warehouse for BI dashboards

blocks.content: The lake is the archive of everything. The warehouse is the polished, trustworthy layer that business users actually look at.
6.2 The lakehouse architecture

A newer pattern, called the lakehouse, tries to blend both. It adds a table format layer, things like Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, or Apache Hudi, on top of the same cheap object storage, giving you ACID transactions and enforced schemas without giving up the lake's low cost and flexibility.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396322804-99264204.png
blocks.alt: A lakehouse architecture blending object storage with a table format layer to serve both BI and ML workloads

blocks.content: The pitch is one copy of the data serving both worlds: analysts run SQL against it like a warehouse, and data scientists pull the same raw files for model training, without a separate pipeline duplicating everything.
7. Real World Systems
7.1 AWS: S3, Glue, and Athena

On AWS, the pattern is extremely common. Raw files land in S3. AWS Glue maintains a data catalog, essentially a schema registry that maps files in S3 to table definitions. Athena then lets you run standard SQL directly against those S3 files, using the Glue catalog to know their structure, without ever loading the data into a separate database.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396322805-923187540.png
blocks.alt: S3 as raw storage, Glue as the data catalog, and Athena as the serverless SQL query engine

blocks.content: 7.2 Azure and Databricks

Azure Data Lake Storage is Microsoft's equivalent, blob storage with a hierarchical namespace layered on top, so it behaves like a proper file system at scale. Databricks was originally built around lake centric processing with Apache Spark, and it's the company that created Delta Lake, the table format that underlies most modern lakehouse deployments.
8. Worked Example: Clickstream Events

blocks.title: The scenario
blocks.text: A product team wants to track every click on their web app. They don't yet know every question they'll want answered from it, so instead of designing a rigid warehouse schema on day one, they land the raw events in a data lake.

blocks.content: 8.1 Landing raw events in the lake
blocks.text: 8.1 Landing raw events in the lake

blocks.content: Every click on the site fires a JSON event: user id, page, timestamp, button clicked, browser info, whatever the frontend happens to send. These events stream through a pipeline and get written, as is, into an S3 raw zone, partitioned by date.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396322806-112487544.png
blocks.alt: Raw clickstream events streaming from the web app and landing in the data lake

blocks.content: Nothing here gets filtered or reshaped. If a new field shows up in the event JSON tomorrow, it just lands too, no schema migration needed.
8.2 Extracting a curated subset for the warehouse
blocks.text: 8.2 Extracting a curated subset for the warehouse

blocks.content: A scheduled job runs nightly, reads the raw JSON from S3, filters out bot traffic, aggregates page views per user per day, and loads that clean, well defined table into the warehouse. Dashboards showing daily active users and top pages query this warehouse table, fast and reliable.
8.3 Data scientists querying the raw lake directly
blocks.text: 8.3 Data scientists querying the raw lake directly

blocks.content: Meanwhile, a data scientist building a churn prediction model doesn't want the aggregated warehouse table. They want every raw event, every field, including ones the nightly job dropped because dashboards didn't need them. So they query the raw lake data directly, using Spark or Athena, to build a training set with full fidelity.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396322806-78910576.png
blocks.alt: A data scientist querying raw lake data directly through a notebook to train an ML model

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396322807-93569412.png
blocks.alt: The full worked example: clickstream events landing in the lake, a job extracting a curated warehouse subset, and a data scientist querying the raw lake directly

blocks.content: 9. Implementation Walkthrough
9.1 Writing raw JSON to S3
Landing a clickstream event in the lake is just a file write, partitioned by date so later queries can skip irrelevant days entirely.

import boto3, json, datetime

s3 = boto3.client('s3')

def write_click_event(event: dict):
    day = datetime.date.today().isoformat()
    key = f"raw/clickstream/dt={day}/{event['event_id']}.json"
    s3.put_object(
        Bucket="company-data-lake",
        Key=key,
        Body=json.dumps(event).encode("utf-8"),
    )

write_click_event({
    "event_id": "evt_9182",
    "user_id": "u_4471",
    "page": "/pricing",
    "clicked": "upgrade_button",
    "ts": "2026-07-09T10:15:00Z",
})

blocks.title: Partition early
blocks.content: Partitioning by date (or by source, or both) up front costs nothing and saves a lot later. Query engines can skip whole partitions instead of scanning every file in the bucket.
9.2 Querying the raw data with Athena
blocks.text: 9.2 Querying the raw data with Athena

blocks.content: Once a Glue crawler (or a manually defined table) knows the shape of that JSON, you can query the raw S3 files with plain SQL, no separate database needed.

CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE clickstream_raw (
  event_id string,
  user_id string,
  page string,
  clicked string,
  ts timestamp
)
PARTITIONED BY (dt string)
STORED AS JSON
LOCATION 's3://company-data-lake/raw/clickstream/';

SELECT page, COUNT(*) AS clicks
FROM clickstream_raw
WHERE dt = '2026-07-09'
GROUP BY page
ORDER BY clicks DESC;

11. Interview Angle

When a system design interview brings up analytics or storage for a new data source, the signal interviewers are listening for is whether you recognize the tradeoff, not whether you can recite the definitions.

["Hear \"we don't know the query patterns yet\" or \"we need to store images and video\" and you should be reaching for a data lake","Hear \"finance needs a consistent daily report\" or \"the schema is stable and well understood\" and a warehouse is the better fit","Mentioning a lakehouse pattern (Delta Lake, Iceberg, Hudi) shows you know these two aren't mutually exclusive in a modern stack"]
items: Hear "we don't know the query patterns yet" or "we need to store images and video" and you should be reaching for a data lake
Hear "finance needs a consistent daily report" or "the schema is stable and well understood" and a warehouse is the better fit
Mentioning a lakehouse pattern (Delta Lake, Iceberg, Hudi) shows you know these two aren't mutually exclusive in a modern stack

blocks.title: Don't forget governance
blocks.content: If you propose a data lake in an interview and stop there, expect a follow up question about how you'd stop it turning into a data swamp. Mention a catalog, naming conventions, and ownership, it shows you've thought past the happy path.
The real skill being tested isn't "lake versus warehouse." It's recognizing which one a given problem actually needs, and knowing that most real systems eventually need both.
